name: Amira Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. These are pictures of the future, not predictions. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy plumbing and heating fittings for Calder Trade Supplies, which serves builders' yards and small plumbing firms. I start with coffee and a pile of supplier catalogues, because I know where everything is in a paper catalogue. Then it's the phone: valves from Italy, copper pipe from Poland, boilers from a German rep I've dealt with for twelve years. I walk the warehouse before lunch so I can see what's actually on the shelf, not what the screen says.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about the job, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being the person a plumber calls when nobody else can find a part. It's satisfying, a bit like being a doctor for pipes. What wears me out is the pressure from head office to do more with fewer people, and the new reporting screens. My husband Luca is a bus mechanic, and we've got Giulia, who's twelve, and Marco, who's nine, plus a mortgage that takes the cushion we should've built.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good luck to them. Those little time-savers don't scare me, because the work I do is knowing the people and knowing the stock. I'd tell the others not to worry, though I'd say it more to settle myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully I'd keep my head down. I don't use any of these AI programs and I'm not planning to start. If they make some reports automatic, I'll do what I'm told, but I'd rather do my own checking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on the same, because the same works. I'd do my rounds, keep my supplier numbers, and keep the paper catalogue up to date. I'd also ask the warehouse team to teach me the new scanning screens one at a time, slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, but steady. Nothing's falling apart, but nothing is getting easier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the small routine automations change for you personally?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The money. We have about three weeks of savings, if that. Luca's wage is steady, but the mortgage is two-thirds of it, and there are hardly any other buying jobs round here if Calder had a rough year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's weighing on you already, even in a world where nothing much changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last winter the boiler broke, and we put it on the card. It took us till autumn to pay it off. That's how close we run, so any dip in work, any cut to my hours, and I'd be in trouble.

say: I'd tell colleagues not to worry, though it **settles me** more than them.
I'd say my value is knowing **people** and stock, not reports.
think: I'll keep my head down and do what I'm told, but I won't use **AI programs**.
With three weeks of savings, any hours cut would put us in trouble.
do: Keep my **supplier numbers** and paper catalogue up to date.
Ask the warehouse team to teach me the new scanning screens **slowly**.
Do my warehouse rounds as always.
feel: **Tired** but steady; nothing falls apart and nothing gets easier.
S0.quote: Last winter the boiler broke, and we put it on the card. It took us till autumn to pay it off.
fieldNote: Amira's **money** worries are the real story here, not AI.
She resists technology by habit and says so without embarrassment.
She says she's steady, but one boiler repair takes her months to recover from.

steps.text: Keep the paper catalogue and supplier phone numbers up to date
Ask the warehouse team to show me the new scanning screens
Wait and see how head office changes the reporting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it won't work as well as they claim. Parts will be faster but they'll miss the odd part numbers, the supplier who changed a pack size without telling anyone. Online I'd keep quiet, because I'd not want to look like I'm afraid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us I'm worried. Price checking and reordering are most of what junior buyers do. If a program does that, Calder won't hire any more of them, and it will look at the senior buyers' salaries too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to make myself the one they can't do without. I'd be the one who knows the exceptions and the rep names, and I'd write it all down in a binder. I'd also let someone younger show me one tool, just one, so nobody says I refused.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit insulted. Twenty years of knowing things, and they want a screen to know them instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of your job do you think a program could take over?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The reordering, the price comparison, the supplier email. What I'd keep is the phone call when a shipment is wrong, because a program can't hear it in a supplier's voice that there's a problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think will decide how this goes at Calder?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Head office, and the consultants they'll hire. They'll arrive with slides, and nobody asks the buyers. I'd go to the meeting and say it plainly.

say: I'd say the tools won't work as well as claimed and will miss **odd details** like pack-size changes.
Online I'd stay quiet so I don't look afraid.
think: Price checking is what junior buyers do, so Calder will hire **none** and then look at senior salaries.
Twenty years of knowing things, and they want a screen to know them.
do: Write down what I know in a **binder**: exceptions, rep names, pack-size quirks.
Let one younger colleague show me **one** tool.
Keep the phone call with suppliers as my strength.
feel: **Uneasy** and a bit insulted that twenty years of knowledge could move onto a screen.
S1.quote: A program can't hear it in a supplier's voice that there's a problem.
fieldNote: Amira expects **cuts** among senior buyers and feels exposed because she refuses new tools.
Her plan is to be the keeper of exceptions, which a system could still capture.
She blames head office and consultants.

steps.text: Write up supplier exceptions and rep contacts in a binder
Ask one younger colleague to teach me a single tool
Cut the family's takeaways and the kids' extra clubs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say nothing for a day. Then I'd say we need a clear plan from the owners, and fast. At home I'd talk to Luca before anyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be lost. I don't use the tools, I've no savings to stand on, and there are so few similar jobs in the area. Two years isn't enough for me to learn what they'd need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. I'd probably try to get as many shifts and overtime as I could, stop every non-essential spend, and ask my mother to help with the kids. I'd look at warehouse supervision or anything with a floor. But I can't promise it'd come to anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, and numb. I'd probably cry in the car park first. I'd feel stupid for not learning these things earlier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What goes through your head the first night after you hear this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lie awake and run the numbers. Three weeks of savings, a mortgage and two kids. I'd be going through what we could sell, what Luca could pick up on the side, and how long my mother could stay with us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about your job, or Luca's, that gives you a bit more time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Luca's bus garage is hands-on, so his job should outlast mine. That helps a bit. But the mortgage is bigger than one wage can carry, and I'd have to stand back and let them see that. It's not much time, but it's something.

say: I'd say nothing for a day, then ask the owners for a clear **plan** fast.
At home I'd talk to Luca before anyone else.
think: I'd be **lost**: no AI skills, no savings and few similar jobs nearby.
Two years isn't enough for me to learn what they'd need.
do: Take every overtime **shift** and stop non-essential spending.
Ask my mother to **help** with the kids.
Look at warehouse supervision or other floor work.
feel: **Scared** and numb; I'd cry in the car park first and feel stupid for not learning sooner.
S2.quote: I'd probably cry in the car park first. I'd feel stupid for not learning these things earlier.
fieldNote: Amira has **no plan**, no cushion and no tool skills, so she meets the panicked definition.
Luca's hands-on job is her only comfort.
She turns to family, her mother, because she has nowhere else.

steps.text: Ask my mother to move in and help with the children
Stop every non-essential spend and take all overtime
Apply for warehouse supervisor jobs at nearby depots

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is more than I thought. At work I'd say let's use it and be sensible. With friends I'd probably say we all need to get on a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us I'd still be frightened. My job goes eventually, and I'm the type who puts things off. But five years is enough to maybe learn one tool and keep a bit of money back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my employer to train me properly, on work time. I'd sit with the younger buyers and learn the basics of the AI tools, because there's no point pretending I can skip it. And I'd save a hundred a month by cutting the extras.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit better than two years, but heavy. It feels like a countdown that's slow enough to hear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years instead of two. Does it feel any different to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The buying system first. Whatever Calder picks, I'd ask to be on it from day one, so I'm not the one learning last. I'd also take any course with a certificate, because on paper I only have the old degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you try to learn first, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marco would be fourteen, Giulia seventeen. I'd want Giulia's university plans to be clear by then, and not dependent on me earning what I do now. We'd be having that talk much earlier.

say: I'd say five years is more than I thought, so let's use it **sensibly**.
I'd tell friends we all need to get on a **course**.
think: My job goes eventually, and I'm the type who **puts things off**.
Five years is enough to learn one tool and keep a bit back.
do: Ask Calder for paid **training** on work time.
Sit with younger buyers and learn the **basics** of the AI tools.
Save a hundred a month by cutting extras.
feel: **Heavy**; a countdown slow enough that I can hear it.
S3.quote: I'd ask my employer to train me properly, on work time.
fieldNote: Amira's resistance softens when she has **time**, and she asks for training.
She is still frightened; she admits she procrastinates.
She brings in family plans, with Giulia's university in mind.

steps.text: Ask Calder for paid training on the new buying system
Take a course with a certificate on evenings
Save a hundred a month by cutting extras
Plan Giulia's university costs with Luca early

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and people should relax and get on with it. But I'd mean it for myself, too, to remind myself not to panic. Online I wouldn't say anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think ten years is survivable, but I'd still feel it coming. I'd be fifty-three, so too old to start from scratch and too young to stop. I'd want something solid by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work on the mortgage first, and pay a little extra each month. I'd learn one new tool each year at work. And I'd keep Luca's work and mine apart, so one doesn't fall if the other does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Almost okay. Ten years feels like weather: you know it's coming but you can still plan your week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years make it feel like a different story?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we have the house paid, that Giulia and Marco have their start, and that I didn't hide from it. I want to say I changed in time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to be able to say in ten years' time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The worry doesn't vanish, because the pay is already tight and the mortgage is a long one. But I'd have time to get it under control, which two years would never give me.

say: I'd say ten years is a long time and people should **get on** with it.
I'd mean it partly to calm myself, and say nothing online.
think: Ten years is **survivable**, but at fifty-three I'm too old to start over and too young to stop.
Pay is already tight, so the worry never fully goes.
do: Pay a little extra on the **mortgage** each month.
Learn one new work tool each year.
Keep Luca's and my **incomes** in different kinds of work.
feel: **Almost okay**; ten years feels like weather I can plan around.
S4.quote: I want to say I changed in time.
fieldNote: Ten years lets Amira move from panic to **slow change**.
Her money pressure keeps her anxious even here.
She sees the family's two incomes as insurance.

steps.text: Pay extra on the mortgage every month
Learn one new buying tool each year at work
Plan with Luca so both incomes are not in one field

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. I'd be lost, with no tool skills, no savings and no other buyer jobs nearby. What would help is paid time to learn at work, a warning from the owners, and some support from the government for the mortgage if my hours went.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people who don't use these tools aren't stupid or lazy. We're just busy, and nobody gives us the time. I'd have learned if somebody had shown me.

headlineQuote: People who don't use these tools aren't stupid or lazy. We're just busy, and nobody gives us the time.
portrait: Amira Rossi, 43, is a senior **buyer** of plumbing parts, with a bus-mechanic husband, two kids and a mortgage.
She's centrist and **resistant**: paper catalogues, phone calls to suppliers, and she never uses AI tools.
She carries real money worry already, about three weeks of savings, so even a quiet AI Plateau leaves her anxious.
She expects buying work to be cut first and has **no plan** in the fastest case, which leaves her panicked.
Time softens her: with five or ten years, she asks for training and a slow plan.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture, because she has no skills, savings or nearby jobs to fall back on.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **time to learn** at work, early warning from owners and mortgage support if hours are cut.
